Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: Homarus gammarus, commonly known as the European lobster or common lobster, is a species of clawed lobster found in the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and certain regions of the Black Sea. This species is closely related to the American lobster, H. americanus. Homarus gammarus can reach a length of up to 60 cm (24 inches) and a weight of 6 kilograms (13 pounds), and is distinguished by its prominent pair of claws. In their natural habitat, these lobsters exhibit a blue coloration, which changes to a "lobster red" hue upon cooking. The mating season occurs during the summer, resulting in the production of eggs that are carried by females for up to a year before they hatch into planktonic larvae. Widely regarded as a delicacy, Homarus gammarus is predominantly harvested using lobster pots, particularly around the British Isles.

Homarus gammarus, commonly known as the European lobster, is a large crustacean that can reach a body length of up to 60 centimeters (24 inches) and weigh as much as 5 to 6 kilograms (11 to 13 pounds). However, lobsters typically caught in lobster pots are generally smaller, measuring between 23 to 38 centimeters (9 to 15 inches) in length and weighing between 0.7 to 2.2 kilograms (1.5 to 4.9 pounds). Like other crustaceans, lobsters have a hard exoskeleton that they must shed to grow, a process known as ecdysis or moulting. Young lobsters may undergo this process several times a year, but as they grow larger, the frequency decreases to once every 1 to 2 years.

The first pair of pereiopods features large, asymmetrical claws. One, known as the "crusher," is larger and equipped with rounded nodules for crushing prey. The other, called the "cutter," has sharp inner edges for holding or tearing prey. Typically, the left claw serves as the crusher, while the right functions as the cutter.

In its natural state, the lobster's exoskeleton exhibits a striking blue hue on its upper side, dotted with coalescing spots, and transitions to a vibrant yellow underneath. The iconic red coloration, commonly associated with lobsters, only emerges post-cooking. This transformation occurs because, during the lobster's life, the red pigment known as astaxanthin is bound within a protein complex. The heat from cooking disrupts this complex, liberating the red pigment and producing the familiar red appearance.

Homarus gammarus, commonly known as the European lobster, finds its closest kin in the American lobster, scientifically named Homarus americanus. These two species share striking similarities and can even be crossbred artificially. However, such hybrids are improbable in their natural habitats due to the non-overlapping ranges of these lobsters. Despite their resemblance, several distinct characteristics allow for their differentiation.

Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity at a carapace length of 80-85 millimeters (3.1-3.3 inches), while males mature at a slightly smaller size. Mating usually occurs in summer between a soft-shelled, recently moulted female and a hard-shelled male. The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months, depending on the temperature, attached to her pleopods. Females carrying eggs, known as "berried," can be found year-round.

Eggs hatch during nighttime, releasing larvae that swim to the water surface where they drift with ocean currents and feed on zooplankton. This larval stage, characterized by three moults, spans 15 to 35 days. Following the third moult, juveniles begin resembling adults and transition to a benthic lifestyle. These juveniles are rarely observed in the wild and remain poorly understood, although they are known for their ability to dig extensive burrows. It is estimated that a mere one out of every 20,000 larvae survives to reach this benthic phase. Upon achieving a carapace length of 15 mm (0.59 inches), juveniles emerge from their burrows to commence adult life.

Homarus gammarus inhabits the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway down to the Azores and Morocco, excluding the Baltic Sea. This species is also prevalent throughout most of the Mediterranean Sea, though absent from the region east of Crete. Additionally, it is found along the northwest coast of the Black Sea. The northernmost populations dwell within the Norwegian fjords, extending into the Arctic Circle.

There are four genetically distinct lobster populations: one widespread and three adapted to local environments due to small effective sizes. Northern Norway lobsters, known as "midnight-sun lobsters," form one population. Mediterranean Sea populations differ from Atlantic Ocean ones. The Netherlands has a unique population, distinct from North Sea or English Channel samples.

Imagine unleashing a million lobster larvae into New Zealand’s waters, hoping they'd thrive. That's precisely what happened between 1904 and 1914 in Dunedin, as part of a plan to introduce the European lobster, H. gammarus, alongside the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. Yet, despite this ambitious effort, the lobsters failed to take root.

Adult Homarus gammarus, commonly known as the European lobster, gracefully inhabits the continental shelf at depths ranging from the gentle embrace of the shore to the shadowy descent of 150 meters (0 – 492 feet), though their ventures seldom extend beyond 50 meters (160 feet). These crustaceans favor the steadfast embrace of hard substrates, be it the rugged stoicism of rocks or the firm resilience of hardened mud. Within these habitats, they carve their homes amidst holes and crevices, emerging under the cloak of night to partake in their nocturnal feasts.

Homarus gammarus is vulnerable to a disease caused by a specific bacterium. This disease often affects American lobsters but has only been observed in captive H. gammarus, where the tanks might have previously housed H. americanus.

Homarus gammarus, a culinary treasure, holds a revered place in gastronomy, its allure immortalized in a seventeenth-century English folk song. Commanding lofty prices, it graces tables in forms fresh, frozen, canned, or powdered. Within its mighty claws and sleek abdomen lies exquisite white flesh, while its cephalothorax offers a feast of edible delights, save the gastric mill and the "sand vein" (gut). This European species, celebrated for its superior taste, fetches prices up to threefold higher than its American counterpart, H. americanus.

Lobsters are primarily captured using lobster pots, though baited lines with octopus or cuttlefish can also lure them for net or hand capture. In 2008, the total catch of H. gammarus in Europe and North Africa was 4,386 metric tons, with 3,462 metric tons (79%) harvested in the British Isles, including the Channel Islands. The minimum landing size for H. gammarus is a carapace length of 87 mm (3.4 in).

H. gammarus, the type species of the genus Homarus, was officially established by Direction 51 from the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Previously, confusion had persisted due to the species being identified under various names, such as Astacus marinus Fabricius, 1775, and Homarus vulgaris H. Milne-Edwards, 1837. Additionally, Friedrich Weber's original description of the genus had been overlooked until rediscovered by Mary Rathbun, invalidating earlier type species assignments for Homarus H. Milne-Edwards, 1837 in favor of Homarus Weber, 1795.

In 1974, Holthuis designated the lectotype of Homarus gammarus, a species of European lobster, from coordinates 57°53′N 11°32′E, near Marstrand, Sweden. This site lies 48 kilometers northwest of Gothenburg. Sadly, both the specimen and its counterpart have vanished over time, leaving a gap in the tangible history of this crustacean.

Frank Headlam was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force, born in Tasmania on July 15, 1914. He joined the RAAF as an air cadet in 1934, specializing in flying instruction and navigation. During World War II, he became the commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron in April 1941, which operated Lockheed Hudsons. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December and engaged Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. After returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam held various staff appointments and training commands, ending the war as a group captain. He passed away on December 23, 1976.

Headlam served as Officer Commanding North-Western Area in 1946 and Director of Training from 1947-1950. During the Malayan Emergency (1950-51), he commanded No. 90 (Composite) Wing and RAF Tengah in Singapore. He acted as Air Member for Personnel in 1957 and 1959-60, receiving the Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. Promoted to air vice marshal, he was Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command (1961-62), AOC No. 224 Group RAF (1962-65) during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (1965-66), and AOC Support Command (1966-67). He became a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965. After serving as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London (1968-71), he retired and died in Melbourne five years later.

After completing a conversion course, Headlam joined the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook, part of No. 1 FTS, operating Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes. In the shadow of World War II, No. 1 Squadron embraced its duty, patrolling the convoy routes and scanning the maritime horizons off southeastern Australia. Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 and became wing commander on 1 July. In the heart of Michigan's Lower Peninsula winds M-82, a state trunkline that gracefully stretches between Fremont and Howard City. Its path meanders through Fremont and skirts the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest, offering travelers a scenic journey. M-82's tale began in the Upper Peninsula, first appearing in 1919, but found its enduring route in the Lower Peninsula during the 1920s. Over the years, its path shifted with various extensions and truncations, reaching as far west as New Era or Hesperia, until finally settling into its current course in the late 1970s.

M-82 begins at a junction with M-120 and B-96, located west of Fremont at a tripoint of county lines. M-120 forms the north-south lines separating Newaygo-Oceana and Newaygo-Muskegon counties, while B-96 runs east-west, marking the Oceana-Muskegon county line, extending due west from the intersection. From this junction, M-82 heads east along 48th Street, traversing rural farms into the community of Fremont. As it enters Fremont, the road becomes Main Street, passing through the downtown area. M-82 then turns south along Stewart Avenue and exits the town, rounding a curve to transition onto 72nd Street, continuing eastward through more farmland. As M-82 approaches Newaygo, the landscape becomes more wooded near the Muskegon River. The highway follows Fremont Street eastward to a junction with M-37, where the two highways merge and run concurrently over the river and into downtown Newaygo on State Street. South of downtown, M-82 separates from M-37, turning east again and running along 82nd Street on the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern terminus of M-82 is at exit 118 on US 131/M-46, located west of Howard City.

In the realm of its maintenance duties, the Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) diligently monitors the ebb and flow of traffic across its sprawling network of roadways. These fluctuations are encapsulated in a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT), a statistical measure capturing the volume of vehicles traversing a specific segment of road on any given day throughout the year. In the year 2009, MDOT's meticulous calculations revealed that the section of M-82 west of Fremont bore witness to the highest traffic density, with a staggering 16,532 vehicles passing daily. Conversely, the stretch east of Newaygo lay in stark contrast, marked by the lowest traffic volume at a mere 4,018 vehicles each day. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that no portion of this particular highway has been designated as part of the National Highway System—an illustrious network deemed crucial to the nation's economic vitality, defense strategies, and overall mobility.

Established in 1926, the current M-82 ran initially from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City, passing through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, replacing M-41. In late 1936, M-46 was extended between Newaygo and Howard City, creating a concurrent M-46/M-82 section to bridge a gap in the M-46 route. By 1938, this section was designated solely as M-46, reducing M-82 to the northern M-37 junction in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was rerouted west of Ferry, extending west to end in Shelby instead of Hart.

In the years 1963 and 1964, the western terminus of the highway underwent a series of transformations once more, this time rerouted to chart a course from Hesperia to New Era, skillfully circumventing Ferry. A pivotal alteration in 1969 reshaped the highway landscape within Oceana County. M-20 gracefully stepped into the role of M-82, stretching westward from Hesperia to conclude at New Era, leaving behind its previous endpoint in Muskegon. Meanwhile, the newly christened M-120 assumed the mantle south of Hesperia, while M-82 found itself confined to the stretch between Hesperia and Newaygo. The highway's embrace widened in 1973 when the eastern extremity was nudged back to Howard City. In a strategic rerouting, M-46 shadowed the US 131 freeway southward from Howard City to Cedar Springs, supplanting M-57 as it threaded between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This maneuver liberated the road from Newaygo to Howard City, bringing it back under the M-82 designation. The final tweak arrived in 1978, severing the concurrency with M-120 in favor of the latter. Consequently, M-82 was elegantly shortened to halt west of Fremont, crystallizing the present-day configuration.

Shikamaru Nara is a fictional character from the Naruto manga and anime series created by Masashi Kishimoto. In the series, Shikamaru is a ninja from Konohagakure and a member of Team 10, which includes Ino Yamanaka and their leader, Asuma Sarutobi. Despite his laziness, Shikamaru possesses exceptional intelligence, a trait that creator Kishimoto finds appealing due to Shikamaru's easygoing nature. Beyond the anime and manga, Shikamaru appears in four feature films and various related media, including video games and original video animations.

Numerous anime and manga publications have discussed Shikamaru's character, highlighting his laziness, intelligence, and leadership transformation. Anime News Network praised his emergence as "an unlikely hero" in Naruto. Shikamaru is popular among Naruto fans, ranking high in several polls. Merchandise such as action figures, key chains, and patches has been released.

Masashi Kishimoto expressed admiration for Shikamaru's easygoing yet genius nature, contrasting it with Sasuke Uchiha's intelligent but abrasive personality. He humorously remarked that if he were a girl, he would marry Shikamaru, predicting the character's likely success in life. During the design process for Shikamaru's Part II appearance, Kishimoto aimed for uniqueness despite using a standard vest common among other ninja in the series. To avoid obscuring Shikamaru's hair, he creatively placed the forehead protector on the character's arm.

Shikamaru's first significant appearance in the series is during the Chunin Exams, a biannual event for ninjas aspiring to rise in rank. He is a member of Team 10, alongside Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka. Despite his unmotivated demeanor and a preference for exerting the least effort possible in life, Shikamaru possesses remarkable intelligence; his teacher, Asuma Sarutobi, assessed Shikamaru's IQ to be over 200. Shikamaru's skills are centered around the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kagemane no Jutsu), famously known as "Shadow Possession Jutsu" in the English TV adaptation. This technique, a hallmark of his clan, allows him to merge his shadow with that of an opponent, immobilizing them and compelling them to mimic his actions. As the series unfolds, Shikamaru learns to manipulate his shadow in novel ways. By Part II, he demonstrates the ability to use multiple shadow-based techniques simultaneously and can elevate his shadow off the ground to interact with physical objects; for example, he can pierce foes with shadow tendrils or employ them to hurl weapons.

Shikamaru approaches the exams with a sense of apathy; during his battle with the Sunagakure ninja Temari, he successfully defeats her but ultimately forfeits the match due to his depleted chakra. Despite this setback, he is the only ninja among his peers to be promoted to the rank of Chunin, as the exam overseers were impressed by his strategic insight and intelligence in the fight against Temari. As a Chunin, Shikamaru is appointed leader of a team tasked with preventing Sasuke Uchiha from defecting to Otogakure. Although Shikamaru's team manages to overcome the Otogakure ninja obstructing their path, Sasuke ultimately escapes.

In Part II of the series, Shikamaru is tasked with finding two members of the criminal group Akatsuki. His team successfully locates them, but during the ensuing battle, the immortal Akatsuki member kills Asuma Sarutobi despite Shikamaru's efforts to protect him. After attending Asuma's funeral, Shikamaru, along with the remaining members of Team 10 and aided by Kakashi Hatake, sets out to avenge their fallen mentor. While the others confront the member's partner, Shikamaru defeats the immortal Akatsuki member and ensures the body is never recovered. Following the confrontation, Shikamaru vows to protect Kurenai and Asuma's newborn daughter. Later, he is assigned to the Fourth Division with Temari and is appointed as a proxy general under Gaara. In the epilogue, fulfilling his aspirations from the series' final battles, Shikamaru becomes an advisor to the Seventh Hokage, Naruto, after marrying Temari and having a son named Nara.

Shikamaru from Naruto appears in seven films: assisting Naruto and Sakura against Haido's utopian ambitions in the second, battling stone soldiers in the fourth, searching for the Land of Sky's base with Kakashi and Sai in the fifth, fighting a chimera beast with Sakura and Sai in the sixth, confronting the demon Satori in the eighth, adopting a strategic role in a Limited Tsukuyomi universe in the ninth, and leading a team to rescue Hanabi Hyuga in the tenth. He also participates in a tournament in the third original video animation. Shikamaru is playable in nearly all Naruto video games, including Clash of Ninja and Ultimate Ninja series, often using unique Shadow Imitation Techniques. His Part II appearance debuts in Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2.

In the luminous tapestry of the literary world, "Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness" emerges, penned with keen insight by Takashi Yano and brought to life through the artistry of Kishimoto. Within its pages, the sagacious Shikamaru steps forth as both protagonist and storyteller, two years beyond the shadow of the Fourth Ninja War. As the narrative unfolds, it delves into Shikamaru's deepening bond with Temari, a poignant journey that extends beyond the confines of the novel, as he grapples with the tender challenge of naming their child, long after the tale's conclusion.

Shikamaru has consistently ranked highly in the Weekly Shōnen Jump popularity polls for the series, frequently securing positions within the top ten and achieving fourth place in one such poll. Meridian, the sixth largest city in Mississippi, United States, serves as the county seat of Lauderdale County and is the principal city of the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. Geographically, it is situated along major highways, located 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi, 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama, 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana, and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Meridian, established in 1860 at the junction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and Southern Railway of Mississippi, developed a robust economy centered around rail transport, becoming a pivotal trading hub. In February 1864, during the American Civil War, General William Tecumseh Sherman significantly damaged the city in the Battle of Meridian.

After the war, the city was rebuilt and entered a "Golden Age," becoming Mississippi's largest city between 1890 and 1930. It emerged as a prominent manufacturing hub in the South, with 44 trains arriving and departing daily. Union Station, constructed in 1906, now serves as a multi-modal center, providing access to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, with an annual average of 242,360 passengers. Although the economy slowed due to the decline of the railroad industry, the city has diversified, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors employing the most people in 2010. According to 2008 census estimates, the city's population is 38,232. However, within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population is 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it reaches 526,500, with labor forces of 104,600 and 234,200 people respectively, driving the city's economy.

The area hosts two military facilities: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, providing over 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian houses the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and the state's first local Department of Homeland Security. Key Field, named after brothers Fred and Al Key who set a world endurance flight record in 1935, is home to the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and supports the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Rush Foundation Hospital is the largest non-military employer in the region, with 2,610 employees.

In the heart of the city, a vibrant tapestry of arts organizations and historic buildings weaves together the cultural fabric of Meridian. The Riley Center, a beacon of artistic expression, stands proudly alongside the Meridian Museum of Art, inviting locals and visitors alike to immerse themselves in creative wonders. The Meridian Little Theatre offers a stage where stories come alive, while the melodic strains of the Meridian Symphony Orchestra resonate through the air, enchanting audiences with their symphonic tales.

Meridian's rich history is also marked by its connection to the Carnegie library legacy. Once, the city was home to two distinct Carnegie libraries, each serving a separate community under the oppressive shadow of segregation. One library catered to the white population, while the other, known as the Carnegie Branch Library, provided a sanctuary of knowledge for African Americans. Although the latter has since been demolished, it remains a poignant reminder of the segregated era and stands as one of the few Carnegie libraries built for black communities in the Southern United States during that time. Through these institutions, Meridian's past and present are intricately woven, telling stories of resilience, creativity, and the enduring power of the arts.

Meridian has been chosen as the future site for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. Jimmie Rodgers, the "Father of Country Music," was born here, and Highland Park features a museum showcasing his memorabilia and steam-era railroad equipment. The park also hosts the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a National Historic Landmark and the only two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. Notable natives include Miss America 1986 Susan Akin, civil rights activist James Chaney, and Hartley Peavey, founder of Peavey Electronics. The federal courthouse in Meridian was the site of the 1966-1967 trial where, for the first time, a white jury convicted a white official for a civil rights killing.

Meridian was once home to the Choctaw Native Americans. In 1830, the United States acquired this area through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, amid the Indian Removal era. Following the treaty's ratification, European-American settlers started relocating to the region.

In the early days of Meridian, Richard McLemore stood as its pioneer, having been granted a substantial parcel of federal land, stretching over approximately 2,000 acres (810 hectares). McLemore envisioned a thriving community and, with this dream in mind, he extended a generous offer to newcomers—free land. His aim was simple: to attract settlers and breathe life into the region. As time unfurled, most of McLemore's expansive tract found a new owner in 1853. It was Lewis A. Ragsdale, a lawyer hailing from Alabama, who purchased the majority of the land. Meanwhile, the remaining 80 acres (0.32 square kilometers) caught the eye of John T. Ball, a merchant from nearby Kemper County. Together, Ragsdale and Ball, now heralded as the founding fathers of Meridian, embarked on a mission to transform their newly acquired lands. They meticulously began plotting lots, laying the groundwork for what would become a burgeoning city.

There was significant competition over naming the settlement. Ball and the city’s industrial residents favored "Meridian," believing it symbolized "junction." Meanwhile, the agrarian residents preferred a name meaning "mad river" in a Native American language, inspired by a nearby creek. Ragsdale suggested "Ragsdale City." To sway opinion, Ball erected a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, alternating the sign between "Meridian" and the Native American name daily. Eventually, the expanding railroads brought an influx of workers who decided the name should remain "Meridian" permanently. The town was officially incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

Meridian was a small village at the outset of the American Civil War in 1861, yet its strategic location at a railroad junction prompted the Confederates to construct several military installations to bolster their efforts in the war. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman led Union troops into the city, executing a campaign of destruction aimed at crippling Confederate logistics. Sherman's forces dismantled the railroads stretching out from the city, demolished an arsenal, and razed massive storehouses, effectively burning much of Meridian to the ground. Reflecting on the thoroughness of the destruction, Sherman reportedly stated, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." Remarkably, despite the extensive devastation, the city’s railroad lines were swiftly repaired and back in operation just 26 working days after the battle. However, the Reconstruction era was marked by strained race relations, culminating in the riot of 1871, which erupted after a fire damaged numerous businesses, further underscoring the volatile social climate of the period.

The town prospered after the Civil War and entered its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910, driven by railroads that facilitated transportation and industrial growth, leading to a population surge. As the population increased, downtown commercial activity expanded. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian was Mississippi's largest city and a major Southern manufacturing hub. Many historic buildings were constructed during this period, including the Grand Opera House (1890), Wechsler School (1894), two Carnegie libraries (1913), and the <unk> Building (1929), Meridian's tallest skyscraper.

So, let me take you back in time. Picture this: the city was really on the move, all thanks to the efforts of a commission government that decided to shake things up. In 1913, they brought in a whopping 90 new industrial plants! Can you imagine the buzz in the air? And then, fast forward to the 1920s—oh boy, the automobile industry was booming. Folks were surely excited about all the new opportunities rolling into town.

Now, you'd think the stock market crash of 1929 and the Great Depression would slow things down, right? But nope, this city kept attracting new businesses like bees to honey! During the Depression, people needed a break from reality, a bit of escapism. That's when the S. H. Kress & Co. building popped up downtown, offering "luxury to the common man." How cool is that? And right there with it, the Temple Theater opened its doors as a movie house, letting folks dive into the magic of film.

Oh, and around that time, 1933 to be exact, the federal courthouse was built as part of a WPA project. So, even during tough times, this city found ways to keep moving forward and provide for its people. Quite the story of resilience, don’t you think?

Following a temporary economic slump at the conclusion of the Depression, the nation became involved in World War II, revitalizing the significance of railroads. Railways were crucial for transporting gasoline and scrap metal necessary for constructing military vehicles, re-establishing Meridian as the central rail hub of the region. This resurgence in prosperity persisted until the 1950s, when the rise in popularity of automobiles and the Interstate Highway System overshadowed passenger railways. Consequently, the downturn of the railroad industry led to substantial job losses, prompting a population decline as workers migrated to other regions.

Amidst the American Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, Meridian served as a hub for the Council of Federated Organizations and several other activist groups. Local resident James Chaney, joined by Northern volunteers Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman, endeavored to establish a community center, conducting classes to empower African Americans to reclaim their voting rights. However, local whites harbored resentment towards these efforts, leading to frequent racial violence. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman journeyed to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to confer with members of a black church that had been bombed and burned. Tragically, the three vanished that night on their return to Meridian. A large-scale FBI investigation ensued, uncovering their murdered bodies two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

In the federal courthouse in Meridian, seven Klansmen, including a deputy sheriff, were convicted of "depriving the victims of their civil rights" in the Mississippi civil rights workers murders trial, while three were acquitted. This marked the first instance of a white jury convicting "a white official in a civil rights killing." The case was reopened in 2005 by the state, leading to the first charges being brought in the case. Edgar Ray Killen was subsequently convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 60 years in prison. To honor Chaney, Meridian later renamed a portion of 49th Avenue after him and established an annual memorial service.

In the 1960s, the construction of highways facilitated easier commuting, prompting residents to relocate from downtown areas to new housing subdivisions located to the north. This migration led to a shift in commercial activities, with strip commercial interests gradually moving into downtown areas. In response, the city took measures to protect its architectural heritage by designating several areas as historic districts during the 1970s and 80s. To formalize these preservation efforts, the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was established in 1979, followed by the creation of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985, both aimed at maintaining and promoting the city's historic character.

Meridian Main Street spearheaded efforts to revitalize downtown, including building a new Amtrak Station in 1997, inspired by the design of the historic station from Meridian's Golden Age. Other projects included renovating the Rosenbaum Building in 2001, Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, and supporting integrated urban design. Alongside The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street helped renovate the historic Grand Opera House in 2006, transforming it into the Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts.

In late 2007, the Alliance for Downtown Meridian inherited the heartbeat of Meridian's Main Street, joining forces with the Meridian Downtown Association to breathe life into the city's core. The Alliance, a guiding star, offered resources and unwavering support, while the Downtown Association animated the streets with vibrant events. Yet, dreams faltered when Mayor Cheri Barry halted plans to rejuvenate the <unk> Building in 2010. Undeterred, the Alliance champions restoration, nurturing specialty shops, lively eateries, and spirited bars, igniting downtown’s pulse day and night. The Downtown Association beckons footsteps with events, while Meridian Main Street nurtures steadfast businesses, weaving a tapestry of revitalized urban spirit.

Due to Meridian's strategic location as a railroad junction, the city experienced significant development, particularly in the hospitality sector. This development was partly driven by the influx of travelers, which led to the establishment of numerous hotels even before Meridian entered its "Golden Age." Notably, significant hotels such as the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue were erected prior to the dawn of the 20th century. The expansion of railroad infrastructure, marked by the construction of the original Union Station in 1906, further catalyzed the proliferation of hotels catering to both passengers and railroad workers. Among these establishments, the Elmira Hotel was built in 1905, followed by the Hotel Meridian in 1907, Union Hotel in 1908, and Terminal Hotel in 1910. In recognition of their historical significance, Union Hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, while Hotel Meridian and Grand Avenue Hotel were designated as contributing properties to the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, its hotels mirrored the aspirations of a booming economy. This was epitomized by the eleven-story Lamar Hotel, constructed in 1927. The Lamar Hotel was recognized for its historical significance and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. Subsequently, it was repurposed as a county annex building. In 1988, it received the designation of a Mississippi Landmark, further cementing its historical importance.
Built in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel stood as a beacon in the African-American business district, a sanctuary for travelers seeking refuge during segregation’s shadowed years.

During the 1960s and '70s, suburban development led most hotels to relocate from downtown. The Riley Center's 2006 rehabilitation sparked demand for a new downtown hotel. Redevelopment of the <unk> Building was proposed, but efforts halted due to changes in city administration. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was established to promote public support for the building's renovation, offering tours and anniversary events.

Since 1985, Meridian has operated under the mayor-council, commonly referred to as the "strong mayor," form of government. In this system, the mayor serves as the chief executive officer, overseeing the administration and day-to-day operations of the city government. The mayor is elected at-large by the city's population every four years. Complementing the executive branch, the city council functions as the legislative body, responsible for setting policy and adopting the city's operating budget on an annual basis. The council comprises five members, each elected every four years from one of the city's five wards, which are designated as single-member districts.

City Hall, situated at 601 23rd Avenue, is recognized on the National Register of Historic Places. The city is led by Mayor Percy Bland, with governance supported by the city council. The council comprises Dr. George M. Thomas from Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Administrative duties are managed by council clerk Pam McInnis. Overall, the city employs a workforce of 570 individuals.

Following the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city established its own Department of Homeland Security (DHS), becoming the sole local DHS within the state. This department is responsible for overseeing a jurisdiction that encompasses nine counties. It received $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other organizations, which enabled the department to initiate training programs for law enforcement officers from other Southern states on passenger rail rescue techniques. Additionally, the department offers civilian classes in basic handgun safety, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearms training. The DHS has played a crucial role during crises, such as Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it facilitated the establishment and support of shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which comprises three teams, each responsible for nine counties.

Headed by Police Chief Lee since 2009, the Meridian Police Department comprises 115 full-time officers, along with part-time and reserve staff. In 2009, the Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, of which 2,000 were felonies. In 2000, crimes reported increased slightly from 2,008 the previous year. Meridian is described as "the safest city in Mississippi with more than 30,000 people." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, located in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian, is operated by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections. Anthony Clayton is the Chief of the Meridian Fire Department, which responded to over 1,600 calls in 2009, including 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service calls.

On the national level, Meridian is located in Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, which has been represented by Gregg Harper (R) since 2009. Lauderdale County, where Meridian is situated, has consistently voted for the Republican candidate in every United States presidential election since 1972. Before this shift to the Republican Party, white voters in the area supported Democratic Party candidates, as Mississippi was a one-party state dominated by Democrats for decades since the late nineteenth century.

The city's growth has been influenced by various social and economic factors. From its founding until 1970, the total population rose in each census, with growth rates ranging from a high of 165% to a low of 0.2%. However, the population decreased in the 1970 census, slightly increased by 1980, then gradually declined until it began rising again in the early 21st century. Between 1980 and 2000, the population dropped by over 14%. By the 2000 census, the city had 39,968 residents with a population density of 885.9 inhabitants per square mile (342.0/km²). In 2008, it ranked as the sixth largest city in the state, and the population increased again by 2010.

Meridian is the main city in the Meridian area, made up of Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale counties with a 2009 population of 106,139. Within a 45-mile radius, the population is 232,900, and within a 65-mile radius, it is 526,500.

In this city, the skies bless the earth with an average annual rainfall of 58.65 inches (1,490 mm), nourishing the landscape throughout the year with fairly balanced showers. March stands as the reigning monarch of moisture, pouring down an average of 6.93 inches (176 mm) of rain, marking its territory as the wettest month. The city often finds itself under the dramatic influence of thunderstorms, which regularly grace the summer months, though not exclusively, as they appear throughout the entire year. Meridian, known for its longstanding dedication to the arts, hosts numerous cultural organizations and events. The Meridian Art League, established in February 1933, was among the city's first art organizations. Initially, art exhibitions were held at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian. In 1949, after renaming to the Meridian Art Association, exhibitions moved to various city locations. The Association later transformed the former Carnegie library at 25th Ave and 7th St into the Meridian Museum of Art, which opened in 1970. The museum offers rotating exhibitions and educational programs for students and adults. Annually, it presents over thirty exhibitions, featuring traditional decorative arts, ethnographic and tribal materials, photography, crafts, and other artworks. The collection includes 18th and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photography, and several sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA), established in 1978, serves as the official arts agency for Meridian and Lauderdale County. MCA administers the Community Art Grants program and organizes the annual festival, multiple workshops, and various special events. It collaborates with numerous local arts organizations, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. 

The Meridian Little Theatre, one of the South's oldest subscription-based community theatres, was constructed in 1932. It entertains over 22,000 guests each season, making it the most attended community theatre in Mississippi, catering to both residents and visitors of Meridian and Lauderdale County. 

The Meridian Symphony Orchestra, established in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and completed its first full season in 1963. In 1965, the orchestra featured its first international soloist, Elena, in performance. Additionally, the orchestra has contributed to the development of the Meridian Public School District's orchestra and strings programs and the formation of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, serving as the conductor since 1991, leads the orchestra. The orchestra will commemorate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The former Grand Opera House in the city was constructed in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg. Initially, it hosted a German company's performance of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron," among many other renowned artists and works. The opera house closed in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression and remained abandoned for nearly 70 years. In 2000, the Riley Foundation, established in 1998, provided a $10 million grant that initiated the building's restoration. An additional $15 million was sourced from city, county, and federal grants. The renovation was completed in September 2006, and the venue was renamed the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center features a 950-seat auditorium for live performances, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting space. It draws over 60,000 visitors annually to downtown Meridian for conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is rightly considered an architectural treasure, being one of the nation's most intact cities from the turn of the last century. Architecture students from across the nation and Canada frequently visit Meridian in groups as part of their coursework, attracted by the city's numerous structures designed by renowned architects. Notably, the only home in the U.S. South designed by Canadian-born architect Louis S. Curtiss, famous for inventing the glass curtain wall skyscraper, remains in Highland Park. The Frank Fort-designed <unk> Building is regarded as one of the finest Art Deco skyscrapers in the U.S., often drawing comparisons to Detroit's famed Fisher Building. Prominent California architect Wallace Neff designed several homes in Meridian, as well as in the Alabama Black Belt, which adjoins the city across the nearby Alabama state line. Neff, who had relatives in Meridian and Selma involved in the thriving railroad industry, accepted commissions in the area when work in California was scarce. His works are mainly found in the lower-numbered blocks of Poplar Springs Drive, where his <unk> Poplar Springs Drive is often compared to Falcon Lair, the Beverly Hills home in Benedict Canyon of Rudolph Valentino. Unfortunately, one of Neff's designs was lost to an Anderson Hospital expansion in 1990, and another in Marion Park was destroyed by fire in the 1950s. The Meridian Post Office, with its interior crafted entirely of bronze and Verde marble, stands out as a fine example of the type of post office structures built in prosperous cities in the 1920s. Originally, it featured <unk> lighting, which was regrettably removed during a 1960s renovation and now resides in private homes on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian has been chosen as the site for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. The Mississippi Legislature endorsed the concept in 2001, and by 2006, pledged $4 million in funding contingent upon private contributors raising $8 million. In September 2007, the city contributed $50,000 towards the project. The center is proposed to be situated on 175 acres at Bonita Lakes, featuring an outdoor amphitheater, an indoor concert hall, and a Hall of Fame dedicated to Mississippi artists. This Hall of Fame will be located downtown in the former Montana's building, which, along with the adjacent Meridian Hotel building, was purchased for $300,000 in July 2010. To promote the Hall of Fame, the center unveiled its Walk of Fame outside the Riley Center in February 2009. The first star honored Jimmie Rodgers, a native of Meridian. In September 2009, the second star was dedicated to B.B. King, a renowned blues musician from Mississippi. On June 1, 2010, authors Tennessee Williams, Eudora Welty, and William Faulkner were added, followed by Sela Ward on June 24, 2010. The center intends to include many more Mississippi-born stars on the Walk of Fame, with names like Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, and Conway Twitty among those considered.

Another prominent venue for large productions in the city is the Shrine Temple Theater. It features a 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, one of only two original Theater Organs remaining in the state. Originally accommodating 1,800 people, the Temple thrived during the silent movie era as one of the largest stages in the United States, second only to New York City's Roxy Theater. Currently, with seating for 1,576, the Temple hosts regional events, live stage shows, plays, concerts, Shrine functions, and public screenings of classic films throughout the year.

Highland Park is home to the Jimmie Rodgers Museum, where visitors can explore the original guitar of "The Singing Brakeman" alongside various memorabilia celebrating his life and career. The museum not only showcases these personal artifacts but also features railroad equipment from the steam-engine era. Surrounding the museum, visitors can find additional tributes, including outside memorials and a vintage steam locomotive on display. 

To further honor Jimmie Rodgers's legacy, a Mississippi Blues Trail historic marker has been installed in Meridian, highlighting the city as his birthplace and underscoring his significant contribution to the development of the blues style in Mississippi. Remarkably, Meridian was the first location outside the Mississippi Delta to receive this distinguished recognition. Complementing this honor, a Mississippi Country Music Trail marker was placed at Oak Grove Cemetery on June 1, 2010, in tribute to Rodgers.

Each May, since 1953, the city has commemorated the anniversary of Jimmie Rodgers's death with a festival, celebrating his enduring influence on music and culture.

In the heart of the park lies a treasured relic from the 19th century—a carousel crafted in 1895 by Gustav Dentzel of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Known as the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, this enchanting ride has delighted visitors since 1909. It holds the prestigious title of a National Historic Landmark, celebrated as the only remaining two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie of its kind anywhere in the world. The carousel's house is particularly unique, being the sole surviving structure built from an original Dentzel blueprint.

To honor this historic gem, the community embarked on an artistic endeavor called "Around Town." This public arts project showcases 62 carousel horses scattered throughout the city and county, each symbolizing the historic carousel. These pieces have been sponsored by local businesses and citizens, while local artists brought them to life with their creativity and skill.

Since 1992, Meridian has proudly hosted the State Games of Mississippi, an annual multi-sport event inspired by the Olympic Games. This organization is a member of the National Congress of State Games, which holds affiliation with the U.S. Olympic Committee. In its inaugural year, 1,200 athletes competed across twelve sports, and since then, over 70,000 athletes have joined the Games. By 2009, participation had grown to over 4,500 athletes competing in 27 sports. Participants in the games have the opportunity to compete in the Southeast Sports Festival, while medalists may advance to the bi-annual State Games of America.

Initially held over one weekend in June, the games expanded to two weekends as more sports were added. The opening ceremonies commence on the third Friday of June in downtown Meridian. Events take place in various sports parks, including Northeast Park, Davidson Complex, and other fields throughout the city. Northeast Park, spanning 85 acres on Highway 39, features ten tennis courts, four softball fields, three soccer fields, an asphalt track, and a large picnic pavilion. Amtrak's Crescent line connects Meridian with cities including New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington D.C., Charlotte, Atlanta, Birmingham, and New Orleans. Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, stands approximately 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) southwest of the city of Meridian. Notably, the airport boasts the longest public runway in the state of Mississippi, measuring 10,004 feet (3,049 meters) in length. Since its establishment in 1930, Meridian Regional Airport has consistently provided service to the community, facilitating connectivity to major destinations. Currently, it offers daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport in Texas, thereby enhancing regional travel options and contributing to the local economy by linking Meridian to significant urban centers.

During the Great Depression, residents of the city considered abandoning the airport due to the financial burdens associated with its maintenance. However, in 1935, Fred and Al Key, who were managing the airport, devised a strategy to sustain its operations. From June 4 to July 1, 1935, the brothers undertook an aerial endurance challenge, flying continuously over the city in their plane, the "Ole Miss." Their remarkable feat of remaining airborne for 27 days, amassing a total of 653 hours and 34 minutes, garnered significant publicity and financial support for the city, thereby preserving the airport's functionality. As a tribute to their contribution, the airport was named Key Field, commemorating the brothers' unbroken flight endurance record in conventional aviation.

Early public education in Meridian was guided by the 1870 Mississippi Constitution. From 1870 to 1885, the Board of School Directors, appointed by the City Council, was responsible for operating the schools. Although several schools existed in the city before 1884, they were privately owned and collectively enrolled only about 400 students. The city constructed its first publicly owned school in September 1884. The first public school for Black students operated in facilities rented from St. Paul Methodist Church. In January 1888, the Mississippi Legislature amended the city charter, allowing Meridian to establish its own municipal school district. Subsequently, in March of the same year, $30,000 in bonds was approved to fund the construction of new public schools. From this bond, the Wechsler School was built in 1894, marking the first brick public school in the state constructed specifically for Black students.

Meridian Public School District expanded from its early beginnings to its current size, featuring six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. In addition to public schools, Meridian hosts several private institutions: Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, the district's primary high school, spans 37 acres with six buildings and 111 classrooms. It serves grades 10 through 12 and enrolls about 1,500 students.
Meridian, with two colleges, thrives. Community College, born 1937, offers free tuition; history of merging, evolving. Mississippi State joins, enriching education.

Meridian's library system began with two Carnegie libraries built in 1913, one for blacks and one for whites. The Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club, founded in the 1880s by local women, initiated fundraising efforts to establish a library, with their collected books forming its initial collection. Israel Marks, a city leader, successfully sought funding from Andrew Carnegie. The black library was built on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church, while the white library was purchased from the First Presbyterian Church. The African American library was the sole such facility in Mississippi until post-World War I and the only Carnegie library for blacks nationwide. In 1967, following the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the libraries were integrated, collections combined, and relocated. The former white library became the Meridian Museum of Art in 1970, while the former African American library was demolished in 2008. The Meridian-Lauderdale County Public Library now serves the community at its current site.

In the bustling heart of the city, The Meridian Star stands as the sole daily newspaper, chronicling life's myriad tales since its inception in 1898. Originally christened The Evening Star, it adopted its current name in 1915, becoming Meridian's exclusive daily publication by 1921. As of March 2010, it boasts a circulation of approximately 12,000 copies, reaching across the vibrant communities of Lauderdale County and spilling over into the neighboring landscapes of western Alabama and eastern Mississippi. This venerable institution remains a beacon of news and stories for its readers, weaving the fabric of local life with each printed page.

In the present day, the Meridian Star stands as the sole newspaper printed in the city, continuing a rich tradition of journalism. Historically, the city has hosted several notable publications that catered to various segments of the community. Among these was the Memo Digest, a significant paper from the 1970s that offered ten to twenty pages focusing on issues pertinent to the African-American community. With a circulation reaching approximately 5,000 readers, the Memo Digest provided a vital voice and platform for discussions relevant to its audience during a dynamic period in history. In addition to the Memo Digest, the city has seen a diverse array of newspapers throughout its history. These include The Colored Messenger, which likely served the African-American community, The State, The Weekly Mercury, The Blade, Weekly Echo, Fair Play, Meridian Morning Sun, Teacher and Preacher, and Clarion. Each of these publications contributed uniquely to the local media landscape, reflecting the varied interests and concerns of Meridian's residents over the years. As the media evolved, these papers provided not only news but also cultural and social insights, shaping the community's understanding of itself and the world. Today, the Meridian Star carries on this legacy, being the city's primary source of printed news.

Papa Stour, one of the Shetland Islands in Scotland, has a population of fewer than twenty people, some of whom immigrated following a residency appeal in the 1970s. Situated west of mainland Shetland and covering 828 hectares (3.2 square miles), Papa Stour ranks as the eighth largest island in Shetland. The sea's erosion of the soft volcanic rocks has formed a remarkable array of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. The island and its surrounding waters support diverse wildlife populations. The island's west side is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the seas around it are a Special Area of Conservation.

Amidst the timeless whispers of history, the island bears witness to ancient narratives etched in stone, boasting numerous Neolithic burial chambers that speak of bygone eras. Alongside these venerable sites lie vestiges of Duke Hakon's abode, a relic from the 13th century, harking back to the Norse occupation that once swept over the isle. In the 1800s, the island's populace burgeoned to over 380 souls, invigorated by the establishment of a bustling fishing station at the locale known as West Voe. Yet, as the years unfurled, this vibrant community gradually dwindled, reaching a nadir of merely sixteen inhabitants in the 1970s. Nevertheless, there has been a gentle resurgence, breathing life anew into this storied land.

Nestled at the southwestern embrace of St Magnus Bay, the enchanting isle of Papa Stour unfurls its rugged beauty, where nature's artistry carves a mesmerizing tapestry of 34 kilometers (21 miles) of jagged, wave-kissed coastline. This wild and wondrous shore is adorned with countless coves, secretive and small, while four grander 'voes' beckon with their own mysterious allure. Amongst these, the serene embrace of <unk> Voe (from the Old Norse, meaning 'harbour bay') offers a sanctuary most sheltered, where the cliffs cradle a natural rock arch, a testament to time's gentle yet persistent sculpting hand. To the east, the welcoming arms of <unk> Voe (aptly named 'house bay' in Old Norse) extend, offering less seclusion but bearing the heart of the island's maritime soul, as it serves as the principal harbor and the ferry's point of embarkation, where journeys are both begun and ended.

Holm and Maiden Stack stand as vigilant sentinels at the southern entrance to the harbor. Holm, a tidal isle, once sheltered a leper colony until the 18th century, although it is now believed that many of those afflicted were victims of a mere vitamin deficiency rather than true leprosy. Maiden Stack's name is steeped in legend dating back to the 14th century. It is said that Lord Thorvald built the diminutive house atop it, the ruins of which still endure, to "safeguard" his daughter from the advances of suitors. Alas, his scheme was thwarted, for when she departed, she was discovered to be with child; in an alternate telling, she and her beloved fisherman successfully fled together. To the north, West Voe, with its inner recess known as 'Unknown Unknown,' serves as the principal voe, while the smaller Unknown Voe is situated immediately to the west.

The primary settlement on the island today is <unk>, situated with a view of <unk> Voe and encircled by in-bye land to the east of the hill dyke, which extends south from West Voe. A belt of glacial moraine, approximately one and a half kilometers long, divides the island to the west. The majority of the remaining area features shallow stony soil, likely originating from glacial till. Peat is almost entirely absent on the island, and the volcanic rocks contribute to relatively fertile soils. This scarcity of peat resulted in 'turf scalping' for fuel, leaving exposed rock areas in the island's interior.

Besides the larger islets surrounding Papa Stour, there are numerous smaller isles and skerries along its coastline. These include Stack, Skerry, Holm, Stacks, Holm of Melby, Koda Skerry, Lyra Skerry, Skerries, Skerry, Sula Stack, Swat Skerry, The Horn, and Wilma Skerry. Additionally, the Ve Skerries are located 5 kilometers (3.1 miles) northwest of Papa Stour. Ve Skerries comprise North Skerry and The Clubb. Positioned between Papa Stour and Ve Skerries is the shallow bank known as Papa.

On 21 June 2008, Stuart Hill, owner and sole resident of the 1-hectare (2.5-acre) island of <unk> Holm, renamed " <unk> Island," declared it a Crown Dependency of <unk>. Hill based this on a 1468 marriage agreement between King Christian of Norway and King James III of Scotland, asserting the island should be a British Crown Dependency, independent of the United Kingdom and the European Union. The United Kingdom did not recognize this claim.

The island presents a fascinating geological tapestry woven from volcanic and sedimentary rock formations dating back to the Devonian period. During this era, the Scottish landmass was part of the Old Red Sandstone Continent, situated around 10 to 25 degrees south of the equator. This positioning contributed to the creation of Old Red Sandstone deposits, formed between 408 and 370 million years ago. These layers emerged as the earlier Silurian rocks were lifted by the tectonic shifts that would eventually form Pangaea, eroded, and then settled into broad river deltas. A notable feature of this landscape was Lake Orcadie, a freshwater lake that adorned the fringes of eroding mountains, extending from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. Papa Stour's current geological makeup is predominantly volcanic, composed mainly of solidified volcanic ash and lava, particularly rhyolite. However, it also harbors a Devonian fish bed at Lamba Banks, adding a unique touch to its geological profile. The island bears the marks of Pleistocene glaciation, evidenced by the numerous large boulders scattered across the landscape, serving as silent witnesses to a bygone icy age.

Papa Stour is a vibrant habitat teeming with diverse wildlife, where marine creatures such as otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises are commonly observed in its waters and along its shores. The island serves as a crucial breeding ground for an array of bird species, including the Atlantic puffin, Arctic and common terns, northern fulmar, common guillemot, razorbill, curlew, wheatear, ringed plover, and the great black-backed gull. Additionally, it is a notable stopover for numerous migratory birds, enriching the island's ecological tapestry.

There are many wildflowers like mountain everlasting, spring squill, and heather. The island's west side is a Site of Special Scientific Interest, and the surrounding seas are a Special Area of Conservation. Shetland Ponies are still bred traditionally.

Human settlement on the island began around 3000 BC. Evidence of this early habitation includes several Neolithic burial chambers called "heel-shaped cairns." Details from the pre-Celtic and Celtic periods are sparse. However, when the Norse arrived, it is probable they encountered a religious community. The island's name originates from "<unk> <unk>," meaning "Big island of the Papar" (Celtic monks), distinguishing it from Papa Little, which is located approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

Papa Stour is the subject of a 1299 manuscript written in Old Norse, the oldest surviving document from Shetland. It recounts a dramatic incident at the house of Duke Hakon Magnusson, who later became King Hakon V of Norway. Near <unk> Voe, a circle of stones marks the remains of a 'ting,' or local assembly, where Lord Thorvald <unk> won a duel after being accused of corruption in the manuscript, earning the title ‘dominus de <unk>.’ The story also mentions his unfortunate daughter. The remains of Duke Hakon's 13th-century house are still visible near <unk> Voe.

In 1469, Shetland came under nominal Scottish control. Despite this change in governance, the Norse 'Lairds of Norway' continued to hold their estates on Papa Stour until the 17th century. By the 16th century, merchants from Bremen and Hamburg had established a summer trading post on the island, purchasing fish from the local fleet. This trade contributed significantly to the local economy. By the 18th century, two Scottish lairds, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick, owned Shetland. They capitalized on the island's rich maritime resources by maintaining a thriving deep-sea fishing industry. This industry operated primarily during the summer months and employed six-oared boats known as 'sixareens.' These boats were adept at navigating the challenging waters surrounding Shetland, ensuring the success and prosperity of the fishing operations.

A tradition claims supernatural forces disrupted the chapel's construction, moving its cornerstones overnight to the present church site. In the 19th century, the fishing station at West Voe was established, and the island's population grew to over 360 residents.
