Ah, Papa Stour, a small Scottish island with a rich but tumultuous history, much like many others in the region. Its population once bloomed in the 19th century, only to wither away over the decades, echoing the fate of places like Mingulay. By 1970, the island school had shut its doors as the number of residents dwindled to a mere sixteen, mostly elderly souls. Yet, hope flickered when an ad in Exchange and Mart sparked a revival; a croft and five sheep were offered freely to newcomers, igniting a rush of applicants. This beacon of opportunity swelled the population to 33 by the 1981 census. Alas, harmony proved elusive. By 2005, discord among islanders led to court battles and departures, shrinking the population back to 20, and the school closed once more. The exodus continued; by early 2008, a family of seven departed, leaving just nine islanders behind. The 2011 census showed a modest recovery, with 15 residents, amidst a broader trend of growth across Scottish islands, which saw a 4% increase to 103,702 inhabitants over the decade. Papa Stour's story is one of resilience amidst the ebb and flow of time and tides.

The Aberdeen trawler Ben Doran met its tragic demise on the Ve Skerries, approximately three miles northwest of Papa Stour, on the evening of March 28, 1930, as it was en route to the village of Scalloway to deliver its catch. At the time of the grounding, weather conditions were relatively favorable; however, it was not until the following day that a passing trawler observed and reported the wreckage. By the time rescue efforts were initiated by the coastguard and local volunteers—given the absence of a lifeboat in Shetland during that period—weather conditions had deteriorated significantly, rendering it impossible to approach the skerries. A request was made for the Stromness lifeboat from Orkney, which was merely 120 miles away, to launch a rescue attempt, but the request was submitted too late to provide any assistance. Tragically, all nine crew members perished in the wreck. Of these, only three bodies were recovered: James Mitchell's remains were returned to Aberdeen, while the bodies of J. Cormack and J.R. were interred in Scalloway.

In February 1940, the cargo ship SS Highcliffe ran aground in fog on <unk> Holm, resulting only in the loss of the ship and its cargo due to clement conditions. In 1967, the Aberdeen trawler Juniper ran aground in Lyra Sound at the base of 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs. The 12-man crew was rescued by the <unk> lifeboat, and the coxswain received the RNLI silver medal for the rescue.

On the stormy night of December 9, 1977, the Aberdeen trawler Elinor Viking, helmed by Alec Flett, succumbed to the treacherous Ve Skerries. The <unk> Lifeboat valiantly arrived but was thwarted by relentless seas in its rescue attempt. Urged by Alec Webster, Coastguard Station Officer at Lerwick, a daring volunteer crew soared to the scene aboard a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter from Sumburgh Airport. Battling fierce winds, they heroically winched the entire crew to safety mere hours after the vessel's grounding. Their bravery was lauded with numerous accolades. No lives were lost, yet this perilous event spurred the erection of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979, illuminating the path to the establishment of today's Search and Rescue helicopter unit at Sumburgh Airport.

However, the island's agricultural diversity extends beyond sheep, encompassing an array of livestock such as cattle, pigs, goats, chickens, ducks, and geese. In addition to livestock, vegetables are cultivated, often in unique plots designed to withstand the elements. These plots, nestled within protective circular walls, are commonly referred to as 'scrubs.' Fishing remains a part of island life, though it is pursued on a relatively modest scale compared to other activities. The island features a post office conveniently located at the pier, serving as a crucial point of connection for the residents, but there is no shop available for everyday goods. Mains electricity was introduced to the island only at the end of the twentieth century, marking a significant advancement in infrastructure. The Papa Stour Project, a Christian-supported housing service, offers accommodation specifically to men grappling with drug and alcohol issues, providing them with a pathway to recovery and stability. These crossings, lasting approximately 45 minutes, accommodate vehicles, although the island itself features only a single short road. For visiting yachts, the island's four main voes offer excellent shelter; however, the strong tides present in both the Sound of Papa and to the northwest demand careful navigation.

It is also the inspiration for <unk>'s poem "Da Sang o da Papa Men," which has become a part of the folk music tradition thanks to <unk> Manson's musical adaptation. The repeated chant in the chorus, "<unk> Foula Doon!" is notably impactful.

The phrase "Foula!" denotes the fishermen's practice of rowing their open boat out to sea until the high cliffs of Foula disappeared from view, positioning the vessel approximately 96 kilometers (60 miles) west of Papa Stour. The term 'tide-lumps' describes unusually large swells formed by the interaction of wind and tide. The piece concludes with a resonant image of fishermen guided back to Papa by the scent across the water, illustrating the poet's ability to evoke vivid sensory impressions. This work gains additional depth from the historical context of Da Horn o Papa's collapse in a storm during the poem's composition, serving as an homage to both a lost way of life and a noted geographical feature.

Slayer's 1986 album Reign in Blood kicks off with the track "Angel of Death," penned by guitarist Jeff Hanneman. The song's lyrics and music draw inspiration from the infamous Nazi doctor Josef Mengele, known for his brutal human experiments at Auschwitz during World War II. Due to its controversial subject matter, "Angel of Death" sparked ongoing allegations of Nazi sympathizing and racism against the band throughout their career.
Despite controversy, "Angel of Death" is on all Slayer's live albums. Critics, like Steve Huey of AllMusic, call it a "classic." It's also featured in several movies.

Slayer guitarist Jeff Hanneman composed "Angel of Death" influenced by Nazi physician Josef Mengele after reading related books during a band tour. He stated, "I bought two books on Mengele, thinking it was disturbing material. When recording the album, that content remained in my mind, inspiring the lyrics for 'Angel of Death'."

In the haunting tapestry of lyrics, the grim legacy of Josef Mengele's macabre experiments unfurls, revealing the chilling depths of human cruelty during World War II at the Auschwitz concentration camp. Dr. Mengele, with a cold detachment that belied any semblance of humanity, subjected his victims—often targeting dwarfs and twins—to a nightmarish odyssey of both physical and psychological torment. These lyrics pierce the soul, shedding light on the ghastly tableau of Mengele's so-called "explorations," where the boundaries of ethics were obliterated with ruthless abandon.

The horrors of Mengele's experiments are brought to life through vivid descriptions: experimental surgeries conducted with the sharp precision of a scalpel, yet devoid of the mercy of anesthesia, leaving his subjects writhing in unspeakable agony. The transfusion of blood between twins becomes a grotesque ritual, a sinister dance of life and death orchestrated by a hand that knew no compassion. Isolation endurance tests pushed individuals to the brink of madness, while gassing and injections with lethal germs painted a portrait of suffering that echoes through time.

Mengele's twisted machinations extended to sex change operations and the brutal removal of organs and limbs, each act a testament to the depths of his depravity. The lyrics leave us grappling with the void of the unspeakable, daring us to confront the darkest corners of human history. In their evocative power, they serve as a solemn reminder of the resilience of the human spirit, even in the face of unimaginable horror.

The line "together, joining heads. Just a matter of time 'til you rip yourselves apart," from the penultimate verse, alludes to the allegation that Mengele stitched twins together, one of whom was deformed. The claim that "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back, their wrists back to back too," was first made by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, the so-called "architect of the Holocaust." Alexander asserted that Mengele "sewed the veins together," effectively transforming them into Siamese twins. This accusation gained further attention when Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary "The Search for Mengele," which has been referenced by several authors, including Gerald Posner, an expert on Mengele.

Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood, faced a delay in its release largely because of the controversial lyrical content of the song "Angel of Death." The band was signed to Def Jam Records, and their distributor, Columbia Records, declined to release the album, citing concerns over its graphic artwork and provocative themes. As a result, Geffen Records took over the distribution, releasing Reign in Blood on October 7, 1986. Despite handling the distribution, Geffen Records chose not to list the album on its official release schedule, reflecting the contentious nature of the album's content and the surrounding controversy.
